analysis.one_liner: Requires people earning over $1 million a year to pay at least 30% of that income in federal taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote in the House Ways and Means Committee, and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a new tax on the very highest earners: any individual with adjusted gross income over $1 million would owe a minimum tax of 30% on the portion of their income above that threshold, after subtracting a share of their charitable giving. The tax would only apply when the 30% floor exceeded what they already pay in regular income tax, the alternative minimum tax, and payroll taxes, and it would phase in gradually. Its stated purpose is reducing the federal deficit. The bill was referred to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be every other taxpayer and future generations, through the deficit reduction the bill's sponsors said it would produce — billions of dollars a year collected from the highest earners [S3]. Some high earners whose effective tax rates currently fall below 30% would owe more, while everyone else's taxes would be untouched. No tax rates or deductions would change for people earning under $1 million.

how_it_helps.text: It requires anyone with adjusted gross income above $1 million (half that for married people filing separately) to pay a minimum effective rate of 30% on income above the threshold, after allowing a share of charitable contribution deductions.

The tax is owed only when the 30% floor exceeds what the taxpayer already pays in regular income tax, the alternative minimum tax, and payroll taxes, minus most tax credits — so it only raises bills for people whose current rate falls below 30%.

Its stated purpose is deficit reduction: the bill's title and resolution both frame the revenue as cutting the deficit 'by billions of dollars a year,' reducing the debt burden carried by future taxpayers.
The $1 million threshold is adjusted for inflation after 2014, so it targets a genuinely high-income group rather than drifting down to more households over time.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on individuals with adjusted gross income above $1 million a year — the roughly highest-earning households in the country — who would owe a top-up tax whenever their total federal rate fell below 30% of income above the threshold. Married people filing separately would face a $500,000 threshold. The tax phases in and accounts for charitable giving, so the burden is blunted at the edges.

drawbacks.text: The revenue goes only toward deficit reduction; the bill funds no services or tax relief for anyone else, so an ordinary family would not see a direct benefit from it.

The minimum rate does not actually close tax loopholes — it stacks a 30% floor on top of them. The bill itself acknowledges this, calling it an 'interim step' and urging broader tax reform to repeal loopholes and simplify the system.
The tax is phased in and applies only to the portion of income above the $1 million threshold, so it raises less money and affects fewer taxpayers than a flat 30% minimum would.

Taxpayers can still shield income through the modified charitable contribution deduction, so households with large itemized charitable giving owe less under the minimum than the headline 30% suggests.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — reducing the deficit by taxing top incomes — is real but diffuse: no household program is funded, so ordinary people would not see a direct personal gain, and the largest gains would show up years later in lower interest costs and preserved federal capacity. The main cost falls on a small number of high-income households. The design is reasonable rather than bold: the charitable-contribution carve-out, the credit-only offset, and the phase-in make it gentler than a flat surtax, and the bill itself concedes it is an interim step, not the loophole-closing reform the House resolution calls for [S3]. Its most serious weakness is not design but fate: the committee with jurisdiction never took it up, so none of the trade-offs were ever publicly tested [S5].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Cicilline (D-RI) and seven original cosponsors introduced the Paying a Fair Share Act of 2013 on February 15, 2013, to reduce the deficit by imposing a 30% minimum effective tax rate on high-income taxpayers.
Eighteen House Democrats eventually signed on as cosponsors; no Republican did.
On the day of introduction, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that writes tax law.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote during the 113th Congress.
The bill expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households — those with annual incomes above $1 million — kept the current tax rates and preferences the bill would have raised, and no deficit reduction was collected from them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Households earning over $1 million a year

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the tax-writing committee during the 113th Congress and never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor, so the full chamber never voted on it.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 18 cosponsors were Democrats, and the House majority — Republicans, who controlled Ways and Means and the floor schedule — never acted on the bill [S4, S5].

industries.industry: Households with adjusted gross income above $1 million
industries.note: The roughly one-in-a-thousand households earning seven figures would owe a top-up tax whenever their combined income, corporate, and payroll tax rate fell below 30%. Because the bill died, their current rates — often lower than that on investment and carried income — stayed intact.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and financial advisory services for high earners
industries.note: A parallel minimum tax with a phased-in threshold and a special charitable-deduction calculation would have created new planning work for clients with incomes near $1 million. The bill's death left the existing rules unchanged.
